cover.title: 50 Most Asked API Interview Questions
cover.subtitle: Backend and SDE interview prep
cover.tagline: For backend and SDE candidates: 50 short answers, each with key points and a diagram, table or snippet
pills: Pagination, filtering, rate limiting and caching
Versioning, file uploads and long-running operations

blocks.q: Q1. What is a REST API and what are its six constraints?
a_bullets: REST is an architectural style: ==resources== named by URLs, handled with standard HTTP methods.
Six constraints define it; the sixth is optional.
**Client-server** splits the UI from the data.
**Stateless**: every request carries all its context.
**Uniform interface** is what makes it feel like REST.

blocks.q: Q2. What is the difference between REST and SOAP?
a_bullets: REST is a ==style== that usually sends JSON over HTTP. SOAP is a ==protocol== with a strict XML envelope.
REST is lighter and cache-friendly.
SOAP has built-in standards like WS-Security.
Pick SOAP for strict enterprise or banking contracts.

blocks.q: Q3. What is the difference between REST and GraphQL, and when do you pick each?
a_bullets: REST exposes many fixed endpoints. GraphQL exposes ==one endpoint== where the client asks for exact fields.
GraphQL fixes over-fetching and under-fetching.
Pick REST for simple CRUD and HTTP caching.
Pick GraphQL for varied clients like mobile and web.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Say REST is a style, not a protocol, then name the constraints you would defend.

items: Use plural names and nest only one level deep
Let HTTP methods carry the verb

blocks.q: Q4. What does it mean that HTTP is stateless, and how do you keep state?
a_bullets: The server keeps ==no memory== between requests. Each request must carry everything needed to handle it.
This lets any server instance answer, so scaling out is easy.
Keep state in a **session** store like Redis, keyed by a cookie.
Or put it in a signed token (JWT) the client sends each time.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: REST = six constraints; stateless is the one interviewers probe. GraphQL trades HTTP caching for flexible queries.

blocks.q: Q5. What is the difference between PUT, PATCH and POST?
a_bullets: ==POST== creates under a collection; **PUT** replaces a whole resource; **PATCH** changes some fields.
POST: server picks the id; PUT names the target URL
PUT sends the full body, omitted fields reset; PATCH sends only changes

blocks.q: Q6. Which HTTP methods are safe and which are idempotent?
a_bullets: ==Safe== never changes server state; ==idempotent== gives the same end state when repeated.
Every safe method is idempotent, not the reverse
PUT and DELETE: idempotent yet not safe
POST is neither, so a blind retry can duplicate
PATCH not guaranteed idempotent, e.g. increment

blocks.q: Q7. What is the difference between 401 and 403?
a_bullets: **401**: not authenticated; **403**: known but not allowed.
401 should carry a `WWW-Authenticate` header naming the scheme
Fix 401 with valid credentials or a fresh token
Retrying 403 with the same identity never helps
Some APIs return 404 instead of 403 to hide a resource

blocks.q: Q8. When do you return 400, 404, 409 or 422?
a_bullets: Pick the code by what went wrong, not by a habit of using 400 everywhere.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Retry-safe means idempotent, so never auto-retry POST. 401 asks who you are; 403 says you may not. Keep 400 for syntax, 422 for rules.

blocks.q: Q9. What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
a_bullets: ==Authentication== proves who you are. ==Authorization== decides what that identity may do.
AuthN runs first: password, OTP or token check
AuthZ runs on every request: roles, scopes, ownership
Failing them gives **401** and **403** respectively

blocks.q: Q10. What is the difference between session-based and token-based authentication?
a_bullets: A ==session== keeps state on the server and gives the client only an ID cookie. A ==token== carries the state itself, signed, so the server stores nothing.
Session: easy to revoke, needs a shared store at scale
Token: stateless, scales across servers and services
Cookies need CSRF care; bearer tokens need safe storage

blocks.q: Q11. How does a JWT work and how is it verified?
a_bullets: A ==JWT== is three base64url parts, `header.payload.signature`. The server recomputes the signature with its key and rejects the token on a mismatch.
Payload holds claims: `sub`, `exp`, `iss`, `aud`
Signed, not encrypted: never put secrets in it
Pin the allowed `alg`; reject `none`

blocks.q: Q12. How do you revoke a JWT or log a user out?
a_bullets: A signed JWT stays valid until `exp`, so revocation needs extra state. Keep access tokens short-lived and ==denylist== the token ID on logout.
Access token 5-15 min, refresh token revocable in DB
Denylist `jti` in Redis with a TTL equal to the time left
Rotate the signing key to kill every token at once

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: AuthN = who, AuthZ = what. Sessions are server state, JWTs are signed client state. Verify the signature, exp and aud. Revoke with short expiry plus a jti denylist.

blocks.q: Q13. What is OAuth 2.0 and what are its four roles?
a_bullets: OAuth 2.0 is a ==delegated authorization== framework: an app gets limited access to your data without ever seeing your password.
**Resource owner**: the user who owns the data.
**Client**: the app asking for access.
**Authorization server**: authenticates the user, issues tokens.
**Resource server**: the API that accepts tokens.

blocks.q: Q14. How does the authorization code flow with PKCE work?
a_bullets: The client sends the user to the auth server, gets a short-lived ==code== back, then swaps it for tokens, proving itself with a PKCE secret.
Client makes a random `code_verifier`, sends its hash as `code_challenge`.
Redirect returns `code` plus `state`; check `state` to block CSRF.
Token call sends `code` and `code_verifier`; a stolen code alone is useless.
Required for SPAs and mobile apps, which cannot keep a secret.

blocks.q: Q15. What is the difference between access tokens and refresh tokens?
a_bullets: An ==access token== is short-lived and sent to the API; a ==refresh token== is long-lived and only used to get new access tokens.
Access token lifetime: minutes, sent as `Authorization: Bearer`.
Refresh token goes only to the auth server, never to the API.
Rotate refresh tokens on every use and revoke on theft.
Short access life limits damage if one leaks.

blocks.q: Q16. What is the difference between OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect?
a_bullets: OAuth 2.0 answers ==what may this app access==; OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds a layer answering ==who is the user==.
OIDC adds an **ID token**, a JWT with `sub`, `iss`, `aud`, `exp`.
Request it with the `openid` scope; `/userinfo` returns profile data.
Never use an access token as proof of login.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Validate the ID token: check `iss`, `aud`, `exp` and the `nonce` you sent.

blocks.title: Key takeaways:
blocks.text: OAuth delegates access, PKCE protects the code, refresh tokens renew short access tokens, and OIDC adds login identity.

blocks.q: Q17. What is CORS and how does a preflight request work?
a_bullets: ==CORS== lets a server tell the browser which other origins may read its responses. Without it, the same-origin policy blocks them.
Origin = scheme + host + port, so `app.io` and `api.io` differ.
A non-simple request (JSON body, `PUT`, custom header) triggers an `OPTIONS` preflight first.
The server answers with `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers, and the browser then sends the real call.
Never combine `Allow-Origin: *` with cookies. Echo an allow-listed origin instead.

blocks.q: Q18. What is the difference between CSRF and XSS, and do APIs need CSRF protection?
a_bullets: ==CSRF== tricks a logged-in browser into sending a forged request. ==XSS== runs attacker script inside your page.
CSRF abuses cookies the browser attaches automatically to every request.
APIs that authenticate with a `Bearer` header are largely immune to CSRF.
Cookie-based API auth does need `SameSite` cookies plus a CSRF token.
XSS defeats CSRF tokens, so escape output and set a CSP.

blocks.q: Q19. What is BOLA/IDOR and how do you prevent it?
a_bullets: ==BOLA== (Broken Object Level Authorization, also called IDOR) means a user changes an ID and reads someone else's object.
Login proves who you are, not that `/orders/1042` is yours.
Check ownership on every object access, server-side.
Take the user ID from the token, never from the request body.
Use unguessable UUIDs as defence in depth only. They don't replace the check.
example_code: -- BOLA: id only, no owner check

blocks.q: Q20. How do you secure a public API end to end?
a_bullets: Layer the defences, because no single control is enough. Each layer below stops a different attack.
**TLS** everywhere, with HSTS, so tokens never travel in clear text.
Authenticate every call (OAuth 2.0 or JWT), then authorise per object and per scope.
Validate input against a schema, and cap body size and page size.
Rate limit per key, log and monitor, and return no stack traces.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: BOLA tops the OWASP API Top 10; name it, then show the owner check.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: CORS is the browser's rule, not your API's firewall. Cookie auth needs CSRF defence. Check object ownership on every request, and layer your defences.

blocks.q: Q21. What is the difference between offset and cursor pagination?
a_bullets: ==Offset== pagination says "skip N rows, give me M". ==Cursor== pagination says "give me M rows after this marker".
Offset is simple and lets users **jump** to page 40.
Cursor stays stable when rows are inserted or deleted mid-browse.
Offset can repeat or skip items when the data changes under it.

blocks.q: Q22. Why does offset pagination get slow, and how does keyset pagination fix it?
a_bullets: `OFFSET 100000` still reads and throws away 100,000 rows, so cost grows with page depth.
==Keyset== remembers the last row's sort key and seeks to it through an index.
Cost stays about O(limit) however deep you go.
The sort key must be **unique**, so add `id` as a tie-breaker.
example_code: ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC

blocks.q: Q23. How do you design filtering, sorting and field selection in a list endpoint?
a_bullets: Put all three in the ==query string== of one collection URL, not in separate endpoints.
Filter by field name, sort with a `-` prefix for descending, and select fields with `fields=`.
Whitelist the allowed fields and operators, and reject unknown ones with **400**.
Index the common filter and sort columns, and cap `limit`.

blocks.q: Q24. What should a paginated response contain?
a_bullets: It holds the ==data array== plus everything the client needs to ask for the next page.
Include `next_cursor` (opaque) and `has_more`, and echo the `limit`.
Offer `total` only if it's cheap, because `COUNT(*)` is slow on big tables.
Optionally add a `Link` header with rel=next and rel=prev.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Offset suits small, stable data; cursor or keyset suits large or live data. Keep the cursor opaque, sort on a unique key, whitelist filters, and return has_more instead of a costly total.

blocks.q: Q25. How do token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed window and sliding window rate limiting compare?
a_bullets: All four cap requests per client; they differ in how they treat ==bursts== and boundaries.
**Token bucket**: tokens refill at a steady rate, each request spends one.
**Leaky bucket**: requests queue and drain at a fixed rate.
**Fixed window** counts per minute, so a burst at the edge can pass 2x.
**Sliding window** counts the last N seconds, so it is smoother but costs more memory.

blocks.q: Q26. How should a server send and a client handle 429 Too Many Requests?
a_bullets: The server rejects the call with ==429== and says when to come back; the client waits, then retries.
Server: always send `Retry-After` in seconds or an HTTP date.
Client: honour it, else use exponential backoff with **jitter**.
Retry only idempotent calls, and cap the number of attempts.

blocks.q: Q27. How do Cache-Control and ETag work together for HTTP caching?
a_bullets: `Cache-Control` says how long a copy is ==fresh==; `ETag` lets the client check a stale copy cheaply.
Within `max-age` the client skips the network entirely.
After expiry it sends `If-None-Match` with the saved ETag.
If unchanged, the server answers **304** with no body.

blocks.q: Q28. Where do you cache in an API stack and how do you invalidate?
a_bullets: Cache at several layers, closest to the user first, and pick an ==invalidation== rule for each.
Layers: browser, CDN, gateway, app memory or Redis, then the database.
Cheapest option: short **TTL**, accepting slightly stale data.
Precise option: delete or update the key on every write.
Versioned URLs or keys avoid purging at all.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Mark per-user responses `Cache-Control: private` so a shared CDN never serves one user's data to another.

items: Rate limit by API key or user, not just by IP
Return `RateLimit-Remaining` so clients can slow down
Cache only safe, idempotent GET responses

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Token bucket allows bursts; 429 needs Retry-After; max-age plus ETag gives 304; cache in layers and invalidate on write.

blocks.q: Q29. What is an API gateway and what does it do?
a_bullets: An ==API gateway== is the single front door for all clients: it routes each request to the right backend service.
It handles cross-cutting work once, so services stay small.
Auth, rate limiting and TLS termination at the edge
Routing, request/response transformation, aggregation
Central logging, metrics and caching

blocks.q: Q30. What is the difference between an API gateway, a reverse proxy and a load balancer?
a_bullets: All three sit in front of servers; they differ in how much they understand about your **API**.
A load balancer spreads traffic across identical instances.
A reverse proxy hides backends, adds TLS, caching, compression.
A gateway adds API logic: auth, quotas, versioned routes.

blocks.q: Q31. How do timeouts, retries and circuit breakers protect an API?
a_bullets: They stop one slow dependency from dragging down the whole system.
==Timeout== caps the wait, so threads are never held forever.
==Retry== with exponential backoff and jitter fixes transient errors; retry only idempotent calls.
==Circuit breaker== trips after repeated failures and fails fast, then probes before closing.

blocks.q: Q32. When do you choose REST, gRPC or a message queue for service-to-service communication?
a_bullets: Pick by coupling and timing: do you need an answer now, or just need the work done?
**REST**: public or simple request-reply APIs, easy to debug.
**gRPC**: fast internal calls, typed contracts, streaming.
**Queue**: async work, spikes and retries without caller waiting.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Name the failure each pattern prevents: timeout stops hung threads, breaker stops cascading failure.

items: Retry only 5xx, 429 and network errors, never 4xx
Keep the caller's timeout above its sum of retries
Run the gateway redundant: it is a single point of failure

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Gateway = one front door; retry only idempotent calls, with backoff and jitter; trip breakers to fail fast; choose sync REST/gRPC or async queues by need.

blocks.q: Q33. What is the difference between webhooks and polling?
a_bullets: With **polling** the client keeps asking "anything new?". With a ==webhook== the server pushes an HTTP POST when an event happens.
Polling wastes calls and adds up to one interval of delay
Webhooks arrive in near real time but need a public HTTPS endpoint
Use polling behind firewalls; add a slow poll to reconcile missed webhooks

blocks.q: Q34. How do you verify that a webhook is authentic?
a_bullets: Sign the raw body with a shared secret using ==HMAC-SHA256==. The receiver recomputes the signature and compares it with the header.
Hash the **raw** bytes, never re-serialised JSON
Compare with a constant-time function
Sign a timestamp too and reject old ones to stop replays

blocks.q: Q35. What is idempotency and how do you implement an Idempotency-Key?
a_bullets: An operation is ==idempotent== if repeating it leaves the same end state as doing it once. The client sends a unique key per logical request.
Server stores key, request hash and the saved response
Same key again returns the stored response, no second effect
Same key with a different body gets 422; keep keys about 24h

blocks.q: Q36. How do you handle webhook retries, duplicates and out-of-order events?
a_bullets: Senders retry on any non-2xx or timeout, so delivery is ==at-least-once==. Make the handler safe to run twice.
Return 200 fast, then process from a queue
Dedupe on a unique event ID in a table with a unique index
Order by event version or timestamp; ignore stale ones, or refetch the resource

items: Reject unsigned or stale-timestamp deliveries with 401
Store the raw payload so failed events can be replayed
Alert when the retry queue or dead-letter count grows

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Webhooks push, polling pulls. Verify the HMAC on the raw body. Idempotency keys make retries safe. Assume duplicates and out-of-order delivery.

blocks.q: Q37. What are the ways to version an API and which is best?
a_bullets: Put the version in the ==URL path==, a header, or a query parameter. URL path is the most common pick.
**URI path**: `/v1/orders`, visible and easy to cache and route.
**Header**: `Accept: application/vnd.app.v2+json`, clean URLs but hidden.
**Query**: `/orders?version=2`, simple but easy to forget.
Best: URL path for public APIs; header for strict REST purists.

blocks.q: Q38. How do you deprecate an endpoint or ship a breaking change safely?
a_bullets: Never break clients silently: ==announce, signal, overlap, then remove==. Prefer additive changes first.
Send `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers on old routes.
Run v1 and v2 side by side for a published window.
Track v1 traffic per client and chase the stragglers.
After the sunset date, return **410 Gone** with a migration link.

blocks.q: Q39. How do you handle large file uploads?
a_bullets: Don't push big files through your API servers: use ==presigned URLs== so clients upload straight to object storage.
Use **chunked/multipart** uploads so a failure retries one part.
Make uploads resumable with a upload ID and part numbers.
Validate size, type and checksum, then scan after upload.

caption.text:
50 API questions they will ask you. 🎯

If you're prepping for a backend or SDE interview, APIs will come up. Every time. So we boiled it down to the 50 most asked questions, each with a short answer, the key points, and a diagram, table or snippet you can actually remember.

Here's what's covered:

📝 REST, HTTP and status codes
🔐 Authentication, JWT and OAuth 2.0
🛡️ CORS and API security
📄 Pagination and filtering
⏱️ Rate limiting and caching
🚪 API gateways and resilience
🔔 Webhooks and idempotency
🔖 Versioning and file uploads
🧪 Testing and monitoring
📈 Scaling APIs
🏗️ Real-world design scenarios

Plus a one-page cheatsheet at the end for the night before.

Save this for your next prep session and send it to the friend who's interviewing this month.

Which API question do you find the hardest? OAuth flows, idempotency, rate limiting, or the design round? Tell us below 👇

Comment “api” to get all the answers as a PDF.
